title: Leading a Church With Money
subtitle: The offering plate is the most spiritual object in the building and the one pastors are most afraid to touch

sections.title: The Subject Jesus Would Not Stop Naming
sections.body:
We will preach on anything before we preach on money. We will preach on sin, on hell, on sex, on the end of the world, and we will do it without flinching. Then the stewardship sermon comes around once a year and we apologize for it before we begin, as though asking the church to part with its money were a thing requiring an apology.

Jesus had no such flinch. He spoke of money more than he spoke of heaven, more than he spoke of prayer. Sixteen of his thirty eight parables turn on possessions. He looked a rich young man in the eye and named the one idol between him and the kingdom, and the man walked away grieving, and Jesus let him go. He did not chase him with a softer ask. He let the cost stand.

Our silence is not reverence. It is fear. We are afraid because money is the place where the congregation's heart is most exposed and most defended, and we suspect, correctly, that to preach it well is to make people angry. So we stay quiet, and the silence does not protect their souls. It abandons them to the one master Jesus said most directly competes with God.

sections.title: The Man Whose Salary Is in the Plate
sections.body:
Here is the knot no seminar untangles for you. The pastor preaches on giving, and the pastor's own paycheck comes out of what is given. You cannot stand at that plate without standing in your own interest, and everyone in the room knows it, and the knowing poisons the asking unless you face it head on.

I have watched this go wrong in both directions. The pastor who will not preach giving at all, because he cannot bear to look like he is feathering his own nest, and so the church gives thinly and the mission starves and his silence costs the kingdom more than his courage ever would have. And the other pastor, the one who preaches money constantly, whose budget always has a crisis, whose appeals always have an urgency, until the congregation can no longer tell the difference between the gospel and a fundraiser.

The only way through the knot is daylight. Take your own hands off your own compensation. Let a committee set your salary with no input from you and publish what they decide. Then, when you preach giving, you preach it as a man with nothing personal to gain in the room, because you have arranged your affairs so that it is true. The congregation can smell self interest at fifty paces. The only deodorant is transparency, and there is no substitute for it.

sections.title: Daylight or Rumor, Choose One
sections.body:
Money kept in the dark does not stay quiet. It breeds. What people are not told, they invent, and what they invent is always worse than the truth, even when the truth is bad.

The church that will not show its books has already lost the argument, because the silence itself is the accusation. I knew a congregation where the giving was handled by one beloved old saint who had counted the offering alone for thirty years and would let no one near it. No one suspected him. They were right not to. But when he died they found the records were a shoebox and a shrug, and three years of accounting had to be reconstructed from memory, and the trust took a decade to rebuild. He was honest. The system was a scandal waiting for a less honest man.

Publish the budget. Show the actuals against it. Let two unrelated people count every offering and let neither of them be the pastor. Have the books reviewed by someone outside the building every single year, even when, especially when, everyone trusts everyone. The point of financial controls is not that you suspect your people. The point is that you refuse to put any of them in a place where a moment of weakness could destroy them and the church together. Transparency is not the absence of trust. It is the protection of it.

sections.title: Generosity Is a Thing You Disciple
sections.body:
A generous church is not born. It is formed, slowly, by a pastor who teaches his people that what they do with their money is what they are doing with their lives, because their money is their life converted into hours and stored.

This is not fundraising. Fundraising asks for the church's money to meet the church's need. Discipleship asks for the church's heart and trusts that the money follows the heart, because Jesus said it does, said where your treasure is your heart will be also, and he had the order of cause and effect deliberate. You do not give because your heart has moved. Your heart moves because you gave. Generosity is not the fruit of a changed heart only. It is one of the tools God uses to change it.

So I do not preach giving to fill a gap. I preach it because the man who never gives is a man whose heart is being quietly colonized by his own accounts, and he cannot feel it happening, and I love him too much to watch it happen in silence. The budget gap is real and giving will close it. But that is not why I ask. I ask because the offering is one of the few places left in a man's life where he can practice, with his hands, the truth that none of it was ever his.

sections.title: Two Masters, and the Plate Between Them
sections.body:
You cannot serve God and money. Jesus did not say it is difficult. He said it is impossible, and he said it to religious people who were sure they had managed it, who loved God and also loved money and saw no war between the two. The war was there. They had simply made a truce by going numb.

The offering plate sits in the aisle every week as a small weekly confrontation with that impossibility. It asks each person the same question, quietly, with no words. Which master. And the answer they give with their checkbook is more honest than any answer they would give with their mouth.

Lead them through it without fear and without self interest, with the books open and your own salary out of your hands, and you will have done one of the hardest pastoral works there is. Not because money is dirty. Because it is holy, and dangerous, and the place where a soul is most likely to be lost while looking entirely respectable.

Do not flinch from the plate. It is the altar where the heart is weighed.
